title: Upstream of the Rice
logline: Below the embankment of a reservoir two thousand three hundred years old, three bathing ponds cut out of bedrock stand empty in deep shade, and the water that once filled them was let straight on into rice fields, so the same water made a sensation first and a crop second, and only one of the two could be kept.
human_question: The stone is still exactly the right shape for it. So where did the feeling go, and was there ever anywhere for it to be?

place.what_kind_of_place: About forty acres of flat, heavily shaded ground directly below the eastern embankment of an ancient reservoir, inside a World Heritage sacred city. It was laid out as a royal park and bathing garden and what is left of it stands at ankle height: two clusters of natural granite boulders, caves under them, stone slabs bridged between boulders where small pavilions once stood, the footings of two octagonal buildings inside a small moated enclosure at the north end, and below the rocks three large bathing ponds cut out of the bedrock with several smaller ones around them. One pond carries a stone chamber on its western side with elephants bathing among lotus carved in relief on it; another has two connected units and a chamber built of slabs. The channels, troughs and cisterns that fed the ponds and emptied them again are cut into the same rock, and the whole arrangement was supplied from the reservoir above through a sluice. Nobody works here, nothing is sold here, and it is not one of the monuments visitors queue for. It is the quietest ground inside the most visited ancient city in the country.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Everything the film needs is within two metres of the camera. Cut granite at close range, which is the real subject: tool marks, a dished and polished lip worn into a pond edge, a right angle held for a thousand years, moss in the seam. Green light, because the tree cover turns the hardest light in the dry zone into something even and underwater. Still water when there is any, holding a whole carved chamber upside down without a ripple. And the elephants among lotus on the chamber wall, which at macro distance are not a monument but a surface somebody enjoyed cutting. There is no reveal, no summit and no figure. The best shot in the film is water a few centimetres deep moving through a stone channel, filmed from a hand away.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, which is the treatment. Over the length of the film the only movements are light shifting through leaves, the skin of standing water, a leaf landing, an insect, a monitor lizard crossing stone, and the water level behind the embankment rising and falling with the year. The one real event the film can hope for is rain: a dry pond holds two centimetres of water for an hour or two and then loses it, and that is the whole arc of the middle of the film. The camera itself does not move except once, and there is almost no cutting.
place.when_it_looks_best: Overcast, and the half hour after rain. The weeks following the north-east monsoon, roughly January to March, when the reservoir above is at its highest and a pond is likeliest to hold standing water. The dry months from June to September give hard light and near-certain dry stone, which is the film's other half and worth a second visit. Inside the tree cover the usable window is the opposite of everywhere else: mid-morning to mid-afternoon, when the light overhead is brutal and here it arrives green and diffused. Nothing in the film needs golden hour except one still frame from the top of the embankment at first light.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A still, quiet film about a piece of engineering built for comfort, and what is left of it. It opens on water to the horizon at eye level, drops two metres into shade, and then works at close range across cut stone for most of its length before ending on water moving through a channel. It is the slowest film in its group by a long way: the fewest cuts, no camera movement to speak of, no crowd, no aerial required, ambient sound rather than voices, and a payoff that is a hand's width of granite instead of a wide reveal. Someone who never hears a word of narration gets a complete piece with a shape of its own, from a lot of water to a little, and from the built thing to the thing it was built for.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration that a feeling is not a thing that can be stored. The voice points only at what is on screen. The stone was cut around a bodily sensation, and the old compendiums count exactly one kind of mind in which plain bodily pleasure occurs, the one that arises when something touches the body; the rest of what we call enjoyment is gladness the mind makes around the sensation. The arrangement survived intact and the sensation did not, because feeling is a mind tasting what it has taken and never was a property of granite or of water. The hydraulics close the argument from the far side: the same water was let on to the rice, where it did something nobody would call pleasure. And twice the voice says what these books do not say, because the film would be dishonest without it: a pleasant feeling is not a fault, and feeling is not the same thing as wanting.

sequence.on_screen: First light at the top of the reservoir embankment. Water to the horizon at eye level, flat, no wind yet, the far bank a grey line. The camera does not move. Held long enough to be uncomfortable.
sequence.voice: This water has been arranged for two thousand three hundred years. The old compendiums this series works from begin their account of feeling with something very plain: feeling is the tasting of whatever the mind has taken hold of, and because every mind takes hold of something, there is feeling in every single one of them. By the way it is tasted there are three, and the books say flatly that there is no fourth. It is pleasant, it is unpleasant, or it is neither.

sequence.on_screen: The film's only geographic move: one cut, down the inner face of the bank and into the trees two metres below the water line. A wide, absolutely static frame of the largest bathing pond cut into the bedrock, roughly ten metres by nine, dry, leaf litter on the floor, the carved chamber on its western side. Held for the whole of the narration.
sequence.voice: Of all the kinds of mind these books count, and they count a hundred and twenty-one, plain bodily pleasure occurs in exactly one. Not a category. One. The mind that arises when something touches the body. Bodily pain gets one as well, and that is the whole of the body's share of the list. This ground was cut, levelled, channelled, shaded and roofed around that single narrow door.

sequence.on_screen: Close, then closer. The worn lip of the pond at a hand's width: tool marks, a shallow dish polished into the granite edge, a seam with moss in it. Then the relief on the chamber wall, elephants among lotus, at macro distance in flat shade.
sequence.voice: The rest of the count goes to the mind. Sixty-two kinds of moment in these books carry gladness. One carries bodily pleasure. So most of what we mean by enjoying something is gladness the mind makes around a sensation, rather than the sensation itself. Whoever cut this could cut for the sensation. Nobody has ever managed to cut the gladness.

sequence.on_screen: The widest frame in the film and the only one with any depth: the three long ponds under old trees, boulders behind them, green light, nobody in shot, nothing moving but leaves. Held for the length of the narration and several seconds past it.
sequence.voice: These books also sort the minds rooted in wanting into eight, and one of the things they sort them by is which feeling is present. Gladness, when what is met pleases. Or plain indifference, when it does not. Then they list what makes such a mind arise one way rather than the other, and the list is surprisingly domestic: temperament, health, patience, habit, the company you are in, the weather, the food. This garden is that list, built. And the books are careful about the list, so this film will be too. Those are tendencies, not fates, and nobody who ever stood in this water is being described here. We do not know one of their minds, and a camera could not have shown it.

sequence.on_screen: The cut channel by which water left the ponds, filmed from directly above, close. Then a long lens through a gap in the tree line: flooded paddy a few hundred metres off, out of focus and then in.
sequence.voice: In the tenth century a king called Mahinda the fourth had the order of this water cut into a stone slab a few hundred metres from this channel. The sluice was opened, and the water went first through the park, then the plantain arbour, then the garden pond, then the lily pond, and then out to the rice. Pleasure sat upstream of food, deliberately, in writing, and nobody was hiding it. These books would not call that a vice if they were asked. One of them even ranks the flat, unexcited kind of wanting as heavier than the glad kind, which is nobody's expectation; the passage gives no reason for it, and the people who read these texts say that ordering needs checking before anybody leans on it.

sequence.on_screen: Rain. The same static frame as the second beat, now with two centimetres of standing water across the pond floor and the carved chamber upside down in it, unbroken. Then the identical frame an hour later, drying in patches.
sequence.voice: There is a sober line in one of these books and it is worth having exactly as it stands. Even pleasant feeling costs something, because it leans on conditions, it rises and falls, and it hurts when it turns. That is a technical remark about how conditioned experience works. It is not a mood, it is not a verdict on anything that happened here, and it is not a claim that this was not lovely.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff, and the smallest shot in the film: water a few centimetres deep running through the cut stone channel, filmed from a hand's distance, the grain and the tool marks of the granite under it. Nothing else in frame. Ambient sound only, no music. If there is no water that year, the same frame dry.
sequence.voice: The stone is still exactly the right shape. Two thousand three hundred years, and the dish worn into that edge still fits a forearm. The sensation is not here. It is not anywhere, and it was never stored, because a feeling is not the kind of thing that can be kept. It is a mind tasting what it has taken, and then not. The water is still here. It went on from this channel and it grew rice, which is the same water doing something nobody would call pleasure. Whatever the feeling was, it was never in the water.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C006 is what this place was built out of and C032 is what the camera can point at. C006 sorts the eight greed-rooted minds partly by which feeling is present: gladness arises when a pleasing object is met [C006-P:L25], and the Pradeepika ties the neutral feeling to a neutral object [C006-P:L74]. What turns that from a proposition into a location is the Pradeepika's list of background conditions for how such a mind arises, which is domestic and physical rather than metaphysical: temperament, health, patience, habit, company, suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52]. A forty-acre royal bathing garden with cut stone tanks, deep shade, carved chambers and a reservoir plumbed into it through a sluice is that condition list executed in granite, and it is still standing. C032 supplies the physics of what the list was aimed at. Feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour, and because every mind takes an object, feeling is present in every mind [C032-P:L43]; by the way it is experienced it is threefold and the Margaya says outright that there is no fourth [C032-M:L5]. Then the counts, which are the reason this site and not another: bodily pleasure has a single seat, the mind that arises at touch [C032-P:L99], bodily pain one more [C032-P:L103], body and mind are counted apart so that a body can hurt while a mind is glad [C032-P:L95–L97], sixty-two minds carry gladness [C032-M:L9] and fifty-five carry the neutral feeling [C032-M:L13], and the four joyful greed-rooted minds are counted squarely among the pleasant-feeling ones [C032-P:L58]. The pair holds because the site holds both halves in one frame: an intact engineered arrangement for one bodily sensation, with the sensation gone.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That feeling is not wanting, and that the stone demonstrates it in a way no argument can. C032 on its own is a table of counts. C006 on its own drifts towards a verdict on a court that cannot answer back. Together they produce the film's finding: a sensation cannot be stored, and that is not a loss and not a moral. The stone kept its shape because shape is what stone keeps; the feeling was a mind tasting what it had taken [C032-P:L43], and there was never a place to put it. The inscribed hydraulics then close the argument from the other side. The water went through the pleasure and on to the crop by written order, which means pleasantness was never a property the water carried downstream; the rice did not get the leftovers of an enjoyment, it got water. The pairing also fences off the two errors this group is most likely to make. The group's own line, that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins, is named in the C032 digest as an editorial compression rather than a sentence in the extracts, so the film never speaks it as doctrine. And 'pleasure is the enemy' is refused outright, because pleasant feeling runs through generous, kind and deeply concentrated minds too and greed can arise with the neutral feeling as well [C006-P:L74]. A place built for cool water on skin is therefore not a vice, and the Margaya's own ranking of flat wanting above glad wanting [C006-M:L19] is the sharpest available argument against narrating it as one.

concept_links.why: The digest's sorting is the film's subject. The eight greed-rooted minds are distinguished, among other things, by whether the feeling present is gladness, which arises on meeting a pleasing object [C006-P:L25], or the neutral feeling, which the Pradeepika ties to a neutral object [C006-P:L74]. What makes this a place rather than a lecture is the Pradeepika's background conditions for how such a mind arises — temperament, health, patience, habit, company, suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52] — because a royal bathing garden is an attempt to set several items on that list at once, in stone, and the attempt survives. Four of the digest's limits are written into the beats rather than left as caution. The conditions are tendencies and not fate and do not map onto genetics or destiny, so beat 4 says so in the voice and no state of mind is attributed to anybody who ever used this water; the digest's related flag, that the claim about the type of rebirth-mind conditioning joy and spontaneity is a doctrinal claim needing an expert check, is honoured by leaving that strand out of the film entirely. The Margaya's ranking of neutral greed above joyful greed [C006-M:L19] is spoken in beat 5 as the unchecked ordering the digest says it is, because the extract gives no commentarial basis for it — and it is the single most useful fact against reading this garden as decadence, since the books themselves do not rank gladness as the heavy case. The wrong-view dial is dropped completely: the digest forbids mapping wrong view onto any community's faith and flags its own example as needing editorial care [C006-P:L33]. And the prompted-or-unprompted dial [C006-M:L5] [C006-P:L44] has no footage here and is not smuggled in; this film's business is the warmth dial only. The digest's caution that the host's generosity must not be confused with the guest's wanting has its equivalent here: engineering is not an appetite, and the film classifies neither.

It carries the film's physics and its payoff. Feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour and is present in every mind because every mind takes an object [C032-P:L43], which is precisely why the sensation this place was cut for could not be left behind in the stone. By the way it is experienced it is threefold, with no fourth [C032-M:L5]. The counts are what make the engineering legible on screen: bodily pleasure occupies one mind, the one arising at touch [C032-P:L99], bodily pain one more [C032-P:L103], body and mind are counted separately [C032-P:L95–L97], sixty-two minds carry gladness [C032-M:L9] and fifty-five the neutral feeling [C032-M:L13], and the joyful greed-rooted minds sit among the pleasant-feeling ones [C032-P:L58]. Beat 6 takes the Pradeepika's addition that all conditioned feeling counts as suffering [C032-P:L111] in the sense that pleasant feeling leans on conditions, rises and falls and hurts when it turns [C032-P:L117], and says in the same breath that this is a technical analysis and not pessimism, which the digest requires; the digest also records that this teaching rests on the Pradeepika alone, since the Margaya extract does not contain it, and the film claims no more for it than that. Three further limits hold. 'Chase good vibes' is refused, because the same extracts count even pleasant feeling as conditioned. 'Pleasure is the enemy' is refused out loud in beat 5, because pleasant feeling runs through wholesome minds as well. 'Neutral means numb' is refused, because the neutral feeling is counted in the most refined meditative minds and not only in greed. The Pradeepika's own wording for the neutral object [C032-P:L75] is not used at all, because the digest flags it as possibly garbled and in conflict with [C006-P:L74] and in need of an expert check. And the concealed-suffering passage [C032-P:L119] is deliberately left out, because it turns on what can only be known by asking somebody, and this film has nobody in it to ask.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a feeling is not a thing that can be stored, and that here this is visible rather than arguable: the arrangement is intact, the stone is the right shape to the millimetre, and there is nothing in it. That pleasantness was never a property of the water, because the same water went on and grew a crop. And that none of this is an accusation. The books being quoted do not treat a pleasant feeling as a fault, they do not rank gladness as the heavy case, and they do not say that feeling and wanting are the same thing.
what_must_be_real: The stone as it is on the day, wet or dry. No water is poured, dammed, diverted, released or carried in for any shot; no pond, channel or cistern is swept, cleared or wetted; if the ponds are dry the film is dry and the last beat is dry stone. Nothing is cleaned, moved, chalked, outlined or handled, and no carved surface is touched by anybody or anything. No reconstruction, no added water in post, no graded-in reflection. Nobody is asked to stand, sit, look, dip a hand, walk through a frame or leave one. Nobody is filmed bathing or in any state of undress anywhere on the site or in the water above it, and nobody is asked or shown entering water. Visitors who happen through a frame are incidental, unidentifiable and never framed as indulgent, acquisitive, greedy or serene: a camera cannot show which mental factor is present and this film does not pretend it can. No observance anywhere on the site or at the temple beyond it is interrupted, restarted or lit. Ambient sound is recorded as it is, with no music laid under the beats. Nothing is said about the carved circular diagram on the rock face, which is not filmed as a mystery and preferably not filmed at all.
position_hint: middle, late: the group's quietest film, and the one that should follow the loud ones. Every other film in this group shows a pleasant feeling inside a crowd; this one puts it in an empty frame and asks where it went. It also needs the earlier films to have set out the anatomy of wanting, so that this one can spend its time saying what a feeling is not. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Narrating a court's decadence, luxury or excess. There is no moral verdict on the ancient court anywhere in this film, and the sources quoted do not supply one: the Margaya's own ranking puts flat wanting above glad wanting [C006-M:L19], which is the opposite of the sermon a bathing garden invites.
Narrating a king's greatness instead, which is the same failure with the sign reversed. The engineering is described and not admired; no superlative about the builders appears in the voice.

Making anybody in frame an example of appetite. A camera cannot show greed, and this group's standing problem is exactly that. No visitor is framed as indulgent or acquisitive, no face carries a point, and the film is built so that it works with nobody in it at all.
Speaking the group's compressed line that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins. The C032 digest names it as editorial compression and not a sentence in the extracts; it is never said as doctrine.
Reading the Pradeepika's conditions for how a mind arises as fate, breeding or genetics [C006-P:L46–L52]; the digest rules all three out, and beat 4 says so on camera.
Touching the wrong-view dial [C006-P:L33]. The digest forbids mapping it onto any community's faith and flags its own example as needing editorial care. It is absent from the film.
Turning the sources' suffering of change into melancholy [C032-P:L111] [C032-P:L117]. It is a technical claim about conditioned feeling, stated as such in beat 6 and not used as a mood.

The site's best-known feature in popular media is a carved circular diagram on a rock face, promoted as a 'star gate' and as evidence of ancient astronauts, lost technology or an antediluvian world map. Any nod to it, even a sceptical or ironic one, imports that literature into the film. Its meaning is not established; it is left out.

Assuming a drone. This is a World Heritage sacred city, archaeological sites here are treated as no-fly without the archaeology department's clearance, and there is a documented arrest in September 2025 for flying near this city's monuments without it. Every shot in this film is a ground shot and the film is designed to survive refusal without losing anything.
Assuming water. Whether the ponds or the channels hold any is unverified, and the payoff must work on dry stone. The temptation to make water happen is the biggest integrity risk on this shoot.

Stillness collapsing into inertia. This film's real danger is not offence but boredom: with this few cuts, every held frame has to earn its length on texture, sound and light, and the close granite work is what pays for the wide ones.

Contact with protected fabric. The ponds, chambers and carved reliefs are the monument, and macro work at a hand's distance is exactly the kind of filming that damages them. No surface is touched, no tripod leg is set on carved stone, and supervision is assumed rather than resented.
drop_if: The ponds, channels and carved chambers cannot be filmed at close range without contact with protected stonework, or close work is not permitted.
The site is fenced, scaffolded or under conservation works so that the cut stone cannot be seen as stone.
The film can only be made with an aerial, or with water introduced, diverted or held for the camera.
The quiet can only be obtained by having the site closed to other visitors for the crew.

There is no paddy in sight of the garden's outflow any more, in which case the fifth beat loses its second half and the inscription's order has to be carried by the channel alone, which is weaker but survivable.

connections.note: IDEA-0013 has taken in the film this record used to hold: a river-valley road disappearing under one red fruit for eight weeks, with sellers holding bunches out at the verge. The two were near-duplicates — roadside stalls on a through road pressing one crop on strangers who had not meant to stop — and the merged record says what neither could alone. That material, and the strand it had earlier absorbed from IDEA-0016, lives there now. This record was freed for a completely different film in a different district, and nothing of the fruit film is kept here.

A flavour that is not kept anywhere, and a sensation that could not be kept anywhere. That film is a whole district at work producing one for six weeks a year; this one is the engineering left standing after one went, with nobody working in it.

The group's other film in this district and its other film about water, so the distinction matters. That one is a working water body before dawn, people floating on it, something being taken out of it and sold. This one is dry-land cut stone in shade, nobody working, nothing to take, and the water is only a memory of an arrangement.

One of three films from the first group set in this same district, and the closest in period. That one is monumental: a great brick colonnade and an enormous stupa, hard geometry, vertical moves, scale as the subject. This one never has a monument in frame, never looks up, and is made of water, cut stone and shade at ground level.

The second of the three first-group films in this district. That one is a sacred hill: an ascent, a stairway, a terrace, a crowd, first light at the top. This one has no ascent and no summit — its single move is two metres downwards — and its crowd is nobody.

The third of the three first-group films in this district. That one is a pair of colossal carved figures ten kilometres apart, long lenses, and a payoff that is a cut between two sites. This one has no figure and one site, and its payoff is a hand's width of worn granite with water on it.

selection.reason: The group's only piece of pleasure architecture and its only silent film: a place engineered around a single bodily sensation, whose stone survived and whose sensation did not, with an inscribed hydraulic order that put the sensation upstream of a crop. It differentiates the group by period, by kind of place and by treatment all at once.

review.note: Repurposed record, and the verdict is reset because the body is new from end to end. The film this record used to hold — a river-valley fruit district in the weeks of its glut, with sellers holding bunches out at the edge of a through road — has been merged into IDEA-0013, which holds the near-identical film of roadside stalls selling one crop to traffic that had no intention of stopping; the rambutan material and the strand it had absorbed from IDEA-0016 are preserved there and nothing of it is kept here, so merged_with is now empty. The reason for the repurposing is the group itself: all fourteen candidates were working places, markets or trades with no historical story running between them, and a group cannot be a monoculture, so this record was moved to a completely different kind of place in a different district and given the group's quietest treatment. The new film is a royal park and bathing garden of about forty acres below the eastern embankment of an ancient reservoir, whose origins are placed in the third century BCE and whose surviving pavilions and sculpture are dated later, between roughly the seventh and the tenth centuries CE. Its history is hydraulic and it is the binding: a tenth-century slab inscription in the name of King Mahinda IV sets the order in which the reservoir's water was to be used — first through the park, then the plantain arbour, then the garden pond, then the lily pond, and only then out to the rice fields around the neighbouring temple — so a king's bathing sat upstream of the food by written instruction, and the same water gave a sensation first and a crop second. C032's count gives plain bodily pleasure a single seat among a hundred and twenty-one kinds of mind, the one that arises at touch, and C006's condition list for how such a mind arises is domestic and physical, which is what a garden of cut stone, cool water and shade actually is. Two thousand three hundred years later the stone is still exactly the right shape and the sensation is not there, because a feeling is a mind tasting what it has taken and not a property of granite or of water — which the downstream rice proves from the other side. The film moralises about none of it: there is no verdict on the ancient court in either direction, the sources' own ranking puts flat wanting above glad wanting, and the group's line that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins is named as editorial compression and never spoken as doctrine. The carved circular diagram on the rock face, which popular media promote as a 'star gate', is kept out of the film and its pseudo-archaeology is named as unsupported in what_is_disputed. Treatment: still water, green light, cut stone at close range, one camera move, ambient sound, and a payoff a hand's width across. New title; both former titles kept in aliases.

suggested_location.region: Anuradhapura District, North Central Province; inside the sacred city of Anuradhapura, on the flat immediately below the eastern embankment of Tissa Wewa and a few hundred metres north of Isurumuniya
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place found that supplies the concepts and the cinema in the same forty acres, and it supplies them at the scale of a hand rather than a monument. The film's philosophical claim is that a sensation cannot be stored, and this site is a two-thousand-three-hundred-year-old machine for producing one bodily sensation — cool water on skin, cut stone, deep shade — which is still standing, still the right shape, and empty. Nothing has to be argued: the ponds are cut out of the bedrock, the channels that fed and drained them are cut into the same rock, the chamber wall carries elephants bathing among lotus, and the sensation the whole arrangement was for is not obtainable from any of it. The history then closes the argument from the far side, because it is hydraulic and it is written down: a tenth-century inscription orders the reservoir's water through the park first and out to the rice last, so the same water produced a sensation and then a crop, which means the pleasantness was never a property the water carried. And the treatment is the group's missing one. Every other film in this group is loud, hot, fast and full of people; this is still water, green light, granite at close range, reflections, almost no cutting and ambient sound. The best shot the place gives is not a reveal but water a few centimetres deep moving through a stone channel, filmed from a hand away, which is also the clearest statement of the concept.
what_to_film: One held frame from the top of the reservoir embankment at first light: water to the horizon at eye level, no movement, no drone.
The single cut down the inner face of the bank into the trees, which is the film's only change of position.
The largest bathing pond in one long static frame from a fixed low position: the cut rectangle, the leaf litter, the carved chamber on its west side.
The elephants-among-lotus relief on the chamber wall at macro distance in flat shade, without contact and without a light.

The worn lip and the tool marks of the cut granite at a hand's width — the dished and polished edge, the right angles, the seams with moss in them. This is the film's payoff material and most of its running time.
The rock-cut channels, troughs and cisterns where water entered and left, filmed from directly above.
The three large ponds and the boulder clusters behind them in one wide still frame under the trees, the only shot in the film with depth.
A pond during and after rain: standing water, the chamber reflected in it whole, then the identical frame drying in patches.
The outflow side of the garden, and through a gap in the tree line, on a long lens, whatever paddy is still worked within sight.
Long, clean ambient sound: water, insects, leaves, birds, the absence of traffic. No interviews, no voices, no music laid under.
Deliberately not filmed: the carved circular diagram on the rock face. It is the site's tabloid attraction and belongs to a literature this film has no use for.
suggested_location.access: Inside the sacred city of Anuradhapura. On foot: from the Isurumuniya car park, cross the Tissa Wewa bund and take the small path into the garden; footpaths also lead in along the bund itself. Travel sources report that the garden is covered by the Anuradhapura sacred-city ticket, quoted at about US$30 for foreign visitors in late 2025, while the neighbouring rock temple charges its own small fee of a few hundred rupees; none of this has been confirmed with the Department of Archaeology and ticketing for a crew is a separate matter entirely. The site is an archaeological protected monument and the ponds, chambers and reliefs are the protected fabric, so close and macro work will need the Department of Archaeology's permission and should be expected to be supervised. Drone: assume refusal and plan for it. Archaeological sites here are treated as no-fly without archaeology department clearance, approvals for aerial work over the sacred city are reported to be rare, and on 17 September 2025 the Anuradhapura headquarters police arrested a man for operating a drone in the vicinity of Ruwanwelisaya without that clearance. The film as written needs no aerial at all: every shot is a ground shot and the payoff is macro.
suggested_location.best_time: The weeks after the north-east monsoon, roughly January to March, when Tissa Wewa is at its highest and a pond is likeliest to hold standing water. Overcast days and the half hour after rain are the film's best light. The dry months from June to September give hard light and near-certain dry stone, which is the film's other half and worth a second visit rather than a compromise. Inside the tree cover the usable window is the reverse of the rest of the city: mid-morning to mid-afternoon, when the light overhead is unusable everywhere else and here arrives green and diffused. Only one shot needs first light, and it is the frame from the top of the bund.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 25 September 2026, none of it verified on the ground or against printed editions. What is reasonably firm across two or more of the sources listed: the garden's position below the eastern embankment of Tissa Wewa and north of Isurumuniya; an extent of about forty acres (sixteen hectares), though one source gives about thirty-five; an origin placed in the third century BCE under Devanampiya Tissa, who also built the reservoir; three large bathing ponds cut in the bedrock below the boulder clusters with several smaller ones around them, described as among the best-preserved artistic ruins of the ancient capital; the largest pond given as roughly thirty-four by twenty-nine feet with a stone chamber about seven by six feet on its western side carved with elephants bathing among lotus; a southern pond of two connected units with a slab-built chamber; boulder clusters, caves, slabs bridged between boulders as platforms, and a small moated precinct with two octagonal buildings at the north end; and the Vessagiriya slab inscription of Mahinda IV (956–972 CE), which names the park and prescribes the order in which the reservoir's water was to be used, ending with the rice fields around Isurumuniya. The inscription was not read in a scholarly edition (Epigraphia Zeylanica); its order of use is taken from secondary accounts that agree with each other in wording, and the Sinhala terms are rendered variously across them, with kelageya given as a plantain arbour in some and a play-house in others. The coordinates are the OpenStreetMap centroid for the mapped park polygon, not a surveyed point, and no elevation is recorded here because no reliable figure was found. Ticket prices and the question of which sites the sacred-city ticket covers come from travel-site summaries encountered in search results and were not confirmed with the Department of Archaeology. Drone rules were taken from the Sri Lanka Police notice and from drone-guidance sites seen in search results; the arrest of 17 September 2025 near Ruwanwelisaya for operating a drone without archaeology department permission appears in the police notice, whose page returned an error when fetched directly, so it is recorded here from the search index of that page and should be re-checked before it is relied on in writing. What could not be established at all: whether the ponds hold water, in which months, and whether the rock-cut channels ever carry any now; the tree species and the state of the tree cover; visitor numbers by hour; and whether paddy is still worked within sight of the garden's outflow. Deliberately excluded: the large popular literature around the carved circular diagram on the rock face, the Sakwala Chakraya, which is promoted as a 'star gate', an interface with extraterrestrials, a piece of lost technology or the world's oldest map, with pages such as amazinglanka's 'Sakwala Chakraya or the STARGATE of Ranmasu Uyana', ancient-origins.net, ancientpages.com, ufofeed.com and howandwhys.com among those seen and not used. None of it is evidence of anything and it is excluded entirely; archaeologists quoted on the record call the stargate claim absurd. What survives scrutiny is only that the carving exists, that H.C.P. Bell recorded it and read it as a simple cosmographical chart, that later readings have included a tantric or meditational diagram and an early map of the world or cosmos, and that its meaning is not established. The claim that it is pre-Buddhist or about five thousand years old is repeated in popular writing and is not supported by anything found here. Independent corroboration of the drone incident near the great stupa was found after these records were written: a press report (Daily FT, 'Drone camera hits pinnacle of Ruwanweli Maha Seya in Anuradhapura') states that a camera drone being flown for an unpermitted shoot struck the pinnacle of the stupa, that police reported no damage to the stupa or its pinnacle, and that the operator was arrested and his equipment seized under the Archaeological Sites of National Importance Act and was to be produced before the Anuradhapura Magistrate's Court. That report does not carry the date, so the specific date of 17 September 2025 still rests on the police notice alone. The substance — an arrest and a seizure under that Act for flying here without permission — is corroborated, and the detail that the aircraft hit the monument is the strongest argument for the ground fallback this film already carries.

historical_thread.story:
The garden lies on the flat ground immediately below the eastern embankment of Tissa Wewa, the reservoir that Devanampiya Tissa (247–207 BCE) built for his capital: a bund about two miles long and twenty-five feet high, holding some five hundred and fifty acres of water, supplying the city and, the sources say, the king's gardens. Roughly forty acres of that flat ground below the bank were laid out as a royal park and bathing garden, and it was used as a royal retreat from the third century BCE until the end of the Anuradhapura kingdom. What stands there now is not a building. It is a rectangle of ground with two clusters of natural granite boulders in it, caves under them, stone slabs bridged from boulder to boulder to carry small pavilions, the footings of two octagonal buildings inside a small moated precinct at the north end, and, below the rocks, three large bathing ponds cut out of the bedrock with several smaller ones around them. They are described in the literature as among the best-preserved artistic ruins of the ancient capital.

The stonework is the reason to go. The largest pond, at the north, is given at about thirty-four by twenty-nine feet, with a stone chamber roughly seven by six feet built against its western side and carved in relief with elephants bathing among lotus. A pond at the south is made of two connected units, one of them with a chamber built of rock slabs that has been read as a changing room; the joined pair has been interpreted as shower baths in which water was thrown or jetted. There are troughs scooped out of the boulders with sockets cut around them where wooden posts stood, and these are the features that the smaller ponds' name points at, because the tenth-century name of the park means the gold-fish park. There is an artificial waterfall with a rock-cut chamber set behind it. And the channels and cisterns that brought water in and let it out again are cut into the same rock as the ponds. The site was under jungle until H.C.P. Bell identified it in 1901; conservation work is dated from 1940 and is associated with S. Paranavitana. The surviving sculpture and structures are dated later than the garden's origin, and the sources consulted do not agree on how much later: the seventh to eighth century, the eighth to ninth, or the tenth.

The piece of history that matters most here is an administrative instruction. A slab inscription at the Vessagiriya cave complex, in the name of King Mahinda IV (956–972 CE), gives the park its recorded name — Ranmasu Uyana, the gold-fish park — and sets out the order in which the reservoir's water was to be used. The water let out of Tissa Wewa through the royal sluice was to go first into the park; then to the kelageya, which the secondary accounts render as the plantain arbour or as the play-house; then to the uyanteya, the garden pond; then to the mahanel-teya, the water-lily pond; and finally out to irrigate the rice fields around Isurumuniya. It is not a description of a pleasure, and it is not a boast about one. It is a schedule. The king's bathing water was upstream of the food supply by written order, and the same water did both jobs in sequence.

One more thing is on the site, and it is famous for the wrong reasons. On a rock face towards the southern side, in one of the caves, there is a circular carving about a metre and three-quarters across, known as the Sakwala Chakraya, the wheel of the universe: concentric circles, an inner circle quartered by crossed lines, and figures that have been read as aquatic animals. Bell, who first recorded it, called it a naively simple cosmographical chart and thought it might show Mount Meru ringed by oceans. Others have read it as a tantric diagram, as an aid to meditation, or as an early map of the world or of the cosmos. Its meaning is not established. Alongside that there is a tradition, repeated in the guidebooks and in some scholarly writing, that this garden is where Prince Saliya met Asokamala, and the relief of the so-called lovers now shown at the neighbouring temple was itself brought there from somewhere else.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concepts ask what a feeling is and what conditions its arising. This site was built to answer both questions in granite, and the answer it gives is an engineering answer, which is why the history does the work no analogy could.

Start with the count. C032 puts plain bodily pleasure in exactly one of a hundred and twenty-one kinds of mind, the one that arises when something touches the body [C032-P:L99], with bodily pain in one more [C032-P:L103], and everything else on the pleasant side of the ledger is mental gladness, which runs to sixty-two [C032-M:L9]. A royal bathing garden is a structure aimed at that single narrow door. The ponds are cut into the bedrock and finished, the chambers are built and carved, the shade is old, and the water came from a five-hundred-and-fifty-acre reservoir through a sluice, which means nothing about the sensation was left to chance. Then C006 supplies the list the garden is made of. The Pradeepika's background conditions for how a greed-rooted mind arises one way rather than another are not metaphysical at all — temperament, health, patience, habit, company, suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52] — and a garden of cool water, cut stone, shade and arranged company is the most literal attempt anyone has left behind to set several of those at once. The film does not need to claim that the attempt worked, or that it was virtuous, or that it was not. It only needs the arrangement to be visible, and it is: complete, intact, correct to the millimetre, and empty.

That emptiness is the argument, and it is not sentimental. Feeling, in these sources, is the tasting of an object's flavour, and it is present in every mind because every mind takes an object [C032-P:L43]. It is therefore not in the object. The stone kept its shape because shape is the sort of thing stone keeps; the sensation was a mind tasting what it had taken, and there was never a place to put it. Two thousand three hundred years later the dished edge of the pond is still the right size for a forearm and there is nothing in it, not because anything decayed, but because a feeling was never among the things the arrangement contained.

The inscription closes the same argument from the downstream side, and this is the part that no other candidate location supplies. The tenth-century slab does not describe anybody enjoying anything. It orders a sequence: sluice, park, arbour, garden pond, lily pond, rice. If pleasantness were a property of water, the fields would have received the remainder of a pleasure. They received water. The same substance that had just been a sensation on somebody's skin went on to be a crop, which is the same water doing something nobody would call pleasure, and the difference lay entirely in what met it. That is the cleanest available demonstration that feeling is a relation and not a quality, and it is documentary: it is what the stone says.

What the binding must not become is a sermon, and the sources themselves block it twice. The Margaya ranks the flat, unexcited kind of wanting above the glad kind [C006-M:L19], which means that on these books' own reckoning the delighted bather is not the heavy case — and the digest adds that this ordering has no commentarial basis in the extract and needs an expert check, so the film says as much out loud rather than leaning on it. And the C032 digest names the group's own framing, that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins, as an editorial compression rather than a sentence in the extracts, while pointing out that pleasant feeling runs through generous, kind and deeply concentrated minds and that greed can arise with the neutral feeling as well [C006-P:L74]. So the doctrine forbids the obvious film. Pleasant feeling is not a fault, feeling is not the same as wanting, and this garden was not a vice. What is left is the harder and better film: a place where the distinction between a feeling and a wanting is the whole subject, because the only thing that can be observed is the arrangement, and a camera cannot see a mind.
what_is_certain: The garden lies below the eastern embankment of Tissa Wewa in Anuradhapura, a few hundred metres north of Isurumuniya, and is an archaeological protected monument.

Tissa Wewa was built by Devanampiya Tissa in the third century BCE; its embankment is given as about two miles (3.2 km) long and twenty-five feet (7.6 m) high, holding about five hundred and fifty acres (220 ha), and it supplied the city and the royal gardens.

The park covers roughly forty acres (sixteen hectares) on the flat below that embankment; it was used as a royal pleasure garden and retreat, its origins placed in the third century BCE in the reign of Devanampiya Tissa (247–207 BCE), and it continued in use to the end of the Anuradhapura kingdom.

Below the boulder clusters there are three large bathing ponds cut in the bedrock and several smaller ones, described in the literature as among the best-preserved artistic ruins of the ancient capital.

The largest pond, at the north, is given as about thirty-four by twenty-nine feet (10.3 by 8.8 m), with a stone chamber of about seven by six feet (2.1 by 1.8 m) on its western side carved in relief with elephants bathing among lotus.
A southern pond consists of two connected units, one of which has a chamber built of rock slabs.

The site contains natural granite boulder clusters, caves, stone slabs bridged between boulders that once carried small buildings, and at the north end a small moated precinct with two octagonal buildings.
Channels, troughs and cisterns cut into the rock fed the ponds and emptied them, and an artificial waterfall with a rock-cut chamber behind it is recorded.

A slab inscription at the Vessagiriya complex, in the name of King Mahinda IV (956–972 CE), gives the park's name as Ranmasu Uyana, the gold-fish park, and prescribes the order of use of the reservoir's water: released through the royal sluice it goes first to the park, then the kelageya, then the uyanteya (garden pond), then the mahanel-teya (water-lily pond), and finally to the rice fields around Isurumuniya.
The site was under jungle until H.C.P. Bell identified its importance in 1901, and conservation work is dated from 1940, associated with S. Paranavitana.

A circular carving about 1.8 m across, called the Sakwala Chakraya, exists on a rock face at the site; Bell recorded it and read it as a simple cosmographical chart, possibly representing Mount Meru surrounded by oceans.

On 17 September 2025 the Anuradhapura headquarters police arrested a man for operating a drone in the vicinity of Ruwanwelisaya without permission from the Department of Archaeology; Sri Lanka Police have publicly urged that permission be obtained before flying near ancient, high-security or religious sites.
what_is_disputed: The extent. Most sources give about forty acres (sixteen hectares); at least one gives about fifteen hectares described as thirty-five acres. The film does not depend on the figure.

The date of what is standing. One account dates the sculpture to the seventh to eighth century CE, another dates the pleasure pavilions and the present structures to the eighth to ninth, and a third says the ruins visible today are mainly tenth century. The third-century-BCE origin and the later date of the surviving fabric are agreed; the century of the fabric is not, and it is left unsettled rather than averaged.

The function readings. That the slab-built chamber was a changing room, that the joined ponds were shower baths in which water was jetted or thrown, and that the boulder troughs with post sockets held ornamental goldfish and water lilies, are all interpretations offered in the secondary literature, not findings. The film treats them as interpretations.

The wording of the inscription. Secondary accounts agree on the sequence but render the Sinhala terms differently, kelageya appearing as a plantain arbour in some and as a play-house in others. The inscription has not been read here in a scholarly edition.

The meaning of the circular carving is not established. Readings on record include Bell's Buddhist cosmographical chart, a tantric diagram, an aid to meditation, and an early map of the world or of the cosmos. No reading here is preferred over another.

The claims made about that carving in popular publishing and television — that it is a 'star gate', an interface with intelligent species from outer space, a relic of lost technology, or the oldest world map, and that it is pre-Buddhist or some five thousand years old — are unsupported. Archaeologists quoted on the record call the stargate claim absurd. None of that literature is used in this record, and the film does not film the carving.

The tradition that this garden is where Prince Saliya met Asokamala is a tradition, repeated in guidebooks and suggested by some writers, and is not established. The relief of the so-called lovers now shown at the neighbouring temple is itself reported to have been brought there from elsewhere.

Whether the ponds and channels hold water today, and in which months, could not be established from any source consulted. It is the single most important unknown in the record because the film's last shot turns on it, and the film is written so that dry stone carries the ending.

unknowns: No permission, access or supervision has been sought. Clearance for close and macro work on protected stonework is unverified and the whole film depends on it.
Whether the ponds hold water at all, in which months, and whether the rock-cut channels ever carry any now. The last beat turns on it and no source consulted answers it.

Aerial permission over a World Heritage sacred city should be assumed refused, and there is a documented arrest in September 2025 for flying near this city's monuments without clearance. The film is built to need none.
The century of the surviving pavilions and sculpture is unsettled in the sources consulted, ranging from the seventh to the tenth.
The exact wording of the tenth-century inscription was not read in a scholarly edition; its order of use is taken from secondary accounts that agree with one another.
Tree cover and species, ambient noise, and whether the site is quiet enough for clean ambient recording at any hour, are all unverified.
Whether paddy is still worked within sight of the garden's outflow, which the fifth beat's second shot needs, has not been checked.
Ticketing, opening hours and whether the site is covered by the wider sacred-city ticket come from travel-site summaries and were not confirmed with the archaeology department.
